q: Refers to all cities regardless of their population density and to municipalities with a population density of at least 500 persons per hectare.
n: The PSA urban area definition covers all cities, regardless of density, and municipalities with a population density of at least 500 persons per square kilometre (as given in the item). Source: PSA/NSO urban classification (NSCB Res. 9, 2003).

q: Under the Local Government Code, a city with at least 200,000 people and annual income of ₱50 million is a:
n: Under RA 7160, a city with at least 200,000 inhabitants and a latest annual income of at least ₱50 million is a highly urbanized city. Source: RA 7160 (Local Government Code), Sec. 452.

q: Which principle bases harmony between building and site on the site's conditions, the building deferring to nature?
n: Deference is the principle in which the building yields to the site, basing their harmony on the site's conditions and nature. Source: Simonds, Landscape Architecture; Lynch & Hack, Site Planning.

q: Which planning approach serves the least fortunate and least represented rather than a general public interest?
n: Advocacy planning (Davidoff, 1965) has planners represent the least fortunate and least represented, rather than an abstract general public interest. Source: Davidoff, Advocacy and Pluralism in Planning (1965).

q: In Lynch's terms, what are the intensive foci to and from which an observer travels?
n: In Kevin Lynch's terms, nodes are the strategic points or intensive foci (junctions, squares) that people travel to and from. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City (1960).

q: Which element dominates most people's image of the city?
n: Lynch found that paths dominate most people's image of the city. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City.

q: What are the major and minor routes people move along?
n: Paths are the channels people move along: streets, walkways, transit lines and canals. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City.

q: Lines of concentrated activity where ways and places are combined and where life and movement are intensified.
n: Streets are lines of concentrated activity where movement (ways) and places combine and urban life is intensified. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City; Jacobs, The Death and Life of Great American Cities.

q: Who wrote The Image of the City?
n: Kevin Lynch wrote The Image of the City (1960). Lynch's study of how residents mentally map Boston, Jersey City and Los Angeles introduced paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks. Source: MIT Press; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Which prominent visual features, seen from far away, help people orient themselves?
n: Landmarks are prominent visual features seen from a distance, external reference points that help people orient themselves. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City.

q: Which Lynch elements are lateral references, not coordinate axes?
n: Edges are linear boundaries such as shores, walls or rail lines. Lynch calls them lateral references, not coordinate axes. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City.

q: Which areas have an identifiable physical, social or cultural character?
n: Districts are sections of the city with an identifiable physical, social or cultural character. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City.

q: According to Kevin Lynch, which of the following is considered to be the most important of the city elements for navigation?
n: Lynch found paths to be the predominant city element for most observers, the main structure of navigation. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City.

q: Responsive environments that focus on details, with a wide vocabulary of visual cues possess.
n: In Responsive Environments, visual appropriateness is a detailed design with a wide vocabulary of visual cues, so people read a place's uses and choices correctly. Source: Bentley et al., Responsive Environments (1985).

q: Which quality makes an environment easy to understand and navigate?
n: Legibility is the quality that makes an environment easy to understand and navigate. Source: Bentley et al., Responsive Environments; Lynch.

q: What aspect of a responsive environment helps create a sense of familiarity and comfort for its users?
n: Personalization lets users adapt and mark their surroundings, creating familiarity and comfort. Source: Bentley et al., Responsive Environments.

q: Which quality gives users a sense of ownership and control over a place?
n: Personalization gives users ownership and control by letting them put their own stamp on a place. Source: Bentley et al., Responsive Environments.

q: Which quality is the diversity of visual elements and uses that gives a place its richness?
n: Variety is the diversity of uses, forms and experiences that gives a place its richness. Source: Bentley et al., Responsive Environments.

q: What are areas whose structures are dilapidated, obsolete and unsanitary, depressing land value?
n: UDHA defines blighted lands as areas whose structures are dilapidated, obsolete and unsanitary, depressing land values. Source: RA 7279 (UDHA), Sec. 3.

q: Determines current housing needs.
n: The housing backlog measures current, unmet housing need (doubled-up households, displaced and homeless). Future need adds new households and replacement. Source: DHSUD/HUDCC housing need methodology.

q: What describes the housing backlog?
o: The gap between acceptable housing units and the number of families
n: The housing backlog is the gap between the number of families and the number of acceptable housing units available. Source: DHSUD/HUDCC housing need methodology.

q: Which factor of urban growth is the excess of in-migration over out-migration?
n: Net migration, in-migration minus out-migration, is the migration factor of urban growth. Natural increase is births minus deaths. Source: PSA; Weeks, Population: An Introduction.

q: What does net migration measure?
n: Net migration measures in-migration over out-migration. Births over deaths is natural increase. Source: PSA; Weeks, Population: An Introduction.

q: Amixed-use community with an average 670 meters distance of a transit stop and commercial core area.
n: Transit-oriented development is a mixed-use community within an average of about 600–700 m (a 10-minute walk) of a transit stop and commercial core. Source: Calthorpe, The Next American Metropolis (1993).

q: Which group of architects and planners promotes New Urbanism worldwide?
n: The Congress for the New Urbanism (founded 1993) promotes New Urbanism worldwide through its Charter. Source: Congress for the New Urbanism (cnu.org).

q: New Urbanism says each neighborhood needs a center within a five-minute walk of all homes, roughly:
n: New Urbanism places each neighbourhood centre within a five-minute walk, about 400 m (a quarter mile), of most homes. Source: Charter of the New Urbanism; Duany & Plater-Zyberk.

q: Which movement promotes walkable, compact, mixed-use, complete communities?
n: New Urbanism promotes walkable, compact, mixed-use, complete communities. Source: Charter of the New Urbanism (CNU).

q: What is buying land at existing-use value ahead of need, to support planned development and socialized housing?
n: UDHA defines land banking as acquiring land at existing-use value ahead of need, for planned development and socialized housing. Source: RA 7279 (UDHA), Sec. 3.

q: What is acquiring land by trading it for land of equal value or for shares in a government corporation?
n: UDHA defines land swapping as acquiring land by exchanging it for land of equal value or for shares in a government corporation. Source: RA 7279 (UDHA), Sec. 3.

q: What is acquiring lots of many owners, by purchase or expropriation, for planned development without individual boundary limits?
n: UDHA defines land assembly as acquiring lots from many owners, by purchase or expropriation, for planned development without regard to individual boundaries. Source: RA 7279 (UDHA), Sec. 3.

q: Which areas are those declared as such under existing laws and executive issuances?
n: UDHA defines areas for priority development as areas declared as such under existing laws and executive issuances. Source: RA 7279 (UDHA), Sec. 3.

q: Which are urban non-agricultural lands with no improvements by the owner, as certified by the assessor?
n: UDHA defines idle lands as non-agricultural urban lands with no improvements by the owner, as certified by the assessor. Source: RA 7279 (UDHA), Sec. 3.

q: Who is known for the Unité d'Habitation and the Radiant City?
n: Le Corbusier proposed the Radiant City and built the Unité d'Habitation in Marseille (1952). Source: Fondation Le Corbusier; UNESCO.

q: Who prepared the County of London Plan of 1943?
n: Patrick Abercrombie, with J.H. Forshaw, prepared the County of London Plan of 1943. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Patrick Abercrombie.

q: The shape of urban cities formed by two corridors of intense development crossing the center.
n: A rectilinear (cross-shaped) urban form results from two corridors of intense development crossing at the centre. Radio-centric forms have many radial arms. Source: Lynch, Good City Form; Gallion & Eisner, The Urban Pattern.

q: A variable of urban decoration where the environment is to have an understandable simple pattern of signs and clues.
n: Unity, an understandable, simple pattern of signs and clues that holds the parts together, makes an urban environment coherent and readable. Source: Gallion & Eisner, The Urban Pattern; Cullen, The Concise Townscape.

q: Which street pattern divides a site into square or rectangular blocks?
n: A gridiron pattern divides a site into square or rectangular blocks. Source: Lynch & Hack, Site Planning.

q: Which is NOT one of Doxiadis's elements of human settlements?
n: Doxiadis's five elements of human settlements are nature, man, society, shells and networks. "Community" is not one of them. Source: Doxiadis, Ekistics (1968).

q: What are Doxiadis's five elements of human settlements?
n: Doxiadis's five elements are nature, man (anthropos), society, shells (buildings) and networks. Source: Doxiadis, Ekistics (1968).

q: The container of man, which consists of both the natural and man-made or artificial elements.
n: In ekistics, the physical settlement is the container of man, made of natural elements and man-made elements (shells and networks). Source: Doxiadis, Ekistics (1968).

q: Which golden era of US urban design featured grand circulation arteries, park networks and clustered civic centers?
n: The City Beautiful era (about 1890–1910, led by Burnham) featured grand boulevards, park networks and grouped civic centres. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, City Beautiful movement.

q: Which urban process began in late-19th-century England, fed by railways, a mobile middle class and housing estates?
n: Suburbanization began in late-19th-century England, fed by railways, a mobile middle class and new housing estates. Source: Fishman, Bourgeois Utopias; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What is a wide band of parks or undeveloped land around a community?
n: A greenbelt is a wide band of parks, farmland or undeveloped land around a community that limits its outward spread. Source: Howard, Garden Cities of To-morrow; UK Green Belt policy.

q: What is grassland used for hay or grazing, often low land beside a stream?
n: A meadow is grassland used for hay or grazing, often low land beside a stream. Source: Merriam-Webster; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Which major problem gave rise to city planning as a discipline?
n: City planning arose as a discipline mainly in response to rapid urban growth during industrialization: overcrowding, disease and congestion. Source: Hall, Cities of Tomorrow; Encyclopaedia Britannica, urban planning.

q: What unit forms the field on which a city's building fabric and public realm unfold?
n: The block is the unit on which a city's building fabric and public realm unfold, framed by streets and filled with lots and buildings. Source: Panerai et al., Urban Forms: The Death and Life of the Urban Block.
